newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia presidential election tipped for June 15.
newsitem.headline: Croatia presidential election tipped for June 15.

text.p: Presidential elections in Croatia, in which incumbent Franjo Tudjman is expected to score an easy victory, will soon be set for June 15, the state-controlled daily Vjesnik said on Tuesday.
The government is likely to announce the date in the next seven to ten days, the usually well-informed Zagreb paper said.

The election would be a walk-over for the 74-year-old president who led Croatia to independence in the 1991-95 war against Serb rebels after the republic seceded from the former Yugoslavia, diplomats and analysts say.
"It is now clear to everyone that Tudjman is going to win," political commentator Davor Gjenero said.

Recent polls showed Tudjman, who is reportedly sick with stomach cancer and may not live to the end of another five-year mandate, could win in the first of two rounds as there is no clear opposition candidate.

"Tudjman is in a position of strength after the April election. The opposition is in such disarray," said one Western diplomat referring to municipal, county and Upper House elections held last month.
The three main opposition parties, running separately in April's vote, suffered serious defeats which led to a series of squabbles and internal power struggles in all of them.
The bad election results split the centrist Social Liberals down the middle over whether to form coalitions with the ruling Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) on the local level or not.

While flamboyant party president Vlado Gotovac opposes any co-operation with the HDZ and has moved closer to the political left and the formerly communist Social Democrats, his predecessor Drazen Budisa urges a more pragmatic approach.

Gotovac was long thought to be the most serious contender for president and a possible joint opposition candidate to run against Tudjman. But a likely defeat now would ruin his chances of becoming president once Tudjman disappears from the scene.

Budisa is expected to stay out of the forthcoming race as he is the only person acceptable as a presidential candidate to both the opposition and the HDZ, which cannot hope to rule alone once Tudjman is gone.
The party's popularity has never matched that of its leader.
"Budisa is not running against Tudjman as long as he has a chance of inheriting him," a diplomat said.

The near certain defeat has made most of the other parties' candidates reluctant to take part in the race, according to reports in the independent press. But diplomats say it is highly unlikely none of them will run as has been rumoured.
"I would find it very strange if one of them did not run," a diplomat said.
